\section[\hi{माफ़} \hi{कीजिए}]{\hi{माफ़} \hi{कीजिए} (māf kījiye) — please forgive me / sorry}

\label{lesson:HI-C09-maaf-kijiye}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} You already know the formal \textbf{\hi{कृपया}} (\emph{kṛpayā}), "please." Hindi's everyday "sorry" is built the same way you build a request: \textbf{name the kindness, ask for it to be done.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{माफ़}} (\emph{māf}) = "\textbf{forgiven, pardoned}" — not a native Hindi word at all! It's borrowed through \textbf{Persian} from \textbf{Arabic} \textbf{\ar{عفو}} (\emph{ʿafw}), "to pardon, efface, wipe away {[}a wrong{]}." Look closely at the spelling: the dot under \hi{फ} (called a \textbf{nuqtā}) turns the plain \emph{pha} sound into \textbf{fa} — Hindi's way of writing sounds that arrived from Persian and Arabic.
  \item \textbf{\hi{कीजिए}} (\emph{kījiye}) = the \textbf{respectful imperative} "\textbf{please do}," from \textbf{\hi{करना}} (\emph{karnā}), "to do."
\end{itemize}

So \textbf{\hi{माफ़} \hi{कीजिए}} is literally "\textbf{please do forgiven{[}-ness{]}}" — \emph{please make {[}this{]} forgiven.} It's the same light-verb move you've already met: naming a state (forgiveness, kindness, compassion) and asking someone to \emph{do} it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be honest about register — and about English creeping in}
\textbf{\hi{माफ़} \hi{कीजिए}} is warm and genuinely everyday — but Hindi keeps a \textbf{more formal, Sanskritic} cousin for writing and ceremony: \textbf{\hi{क्षमा} \hi{करें}} (\emph{kṣamā karēṁ}), "please grant \textbf{kṣamā}" — from Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{क्षमा}} (\emph{kṣamā}), "patience, forbearance, forgiveness." Where \emph{kṛpayā} was the bookish "please," \textbf{kṣamā karēṁ} is the bookish "sorry."

And here's the honest twist: in casual conversation, many Hindi speakers simply say the \textbf{English word "sorry"} outright — it has been fully adopted into everyday Hindi, the same way English "please" sometimes stands in for \emph{kṛpayā}.

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "māf" — forgiven — then "kījiye," please do{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the whole phrase — "māf kījiye" = please forgive me{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the formal cousin — "kṣamā karēṁ"{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{\hi{माफ़} \hi{कीजिए}} literally mean? (\textbf{"Please do forgiven{[}-ness{]}"} — \emph{māf} "forgiven" + \emph{kījiye} "please do.") Where does \emph{māf} come from? (\textbf{Borrowed via Persian from Arabic} \emph{ʿafw}, "to pardon.") What's the more formal, Sanskritic cousin? (\textbf{\hi{क्षमा} \hi{करें}} \emph{kṣamā karēṁ}, from \emph{kṣamā} "patience/forgiveness.") What do many Hindi speakers just say instead, casually? (\textbf{The English word "sorry."})
\end{tcolorbox}
